title: How to Choose the Right Industrial Degreaser for Your Facility
summary: Selecting the wrong degreaser can cost your facility time, money, and compliance headaches. This guide walks through the key factors to evaluate before making your choice.
content:
Industrial degreasers are not one-size-fits-all products. The right choice depends on the type of soiling, the substrate being cleaned, environmental regulations, and the cleaning method available to your team. Before purchasing in bulk, it is worth spending time understanding the chemistry and evaluating a few key variables.

The first factor to consider is the type of contamination you are dealing with. Light mineral oils and fingerprints respond well to neutral or mildly alkaline cleaners. Heavy carbonized grease, cutting fluids, and polymerized oils require a strongly alkaline or solvent-based degreaser. Applying a mild product to heavy contamination simply means more labor and more chemical — an expensive and time-consuming combination.

Substrate compatibility is equally critical. Alkaline degreasers can damage aluminium, zinc, and certain soft alloys if used at high concentrations. Always check the technical data sheet for compatibility with the materials in your facility. If you are cleaning sensitive painted surfaces or precision-machined components, a pH-neutral solvent-free degreaser is the safest choice, even if it requires slightly more dwell time.

Finally, consider your environmental and regulatory obligations. Many facilities are now required to use biodegradable, low-VOC formulations to comply with wastewater treatment discharge limits and occupational health regulations. Water-based alkaline degreasers generally have a lower environmental impact than solvent-based alternatives and are increasingly the preferred choice for facilities working toward ISO 14001 certification.

title: Extending Equipment Life with a Preventive Lubrication Programme
summary: A well-structured lubrication programme is one of the highest-return investments a maintenance team can make. Here is how to build one that works.
content:
Unplanned equipment downtime costs manufacturing facilities an average of hundreds of thousands of dollars per year. A significant proportion of these failures are directly attributable to inadequate or incorrect lubrication. The good news is that implementing a structured preventive lubrication programme is relatively straightforward and delivers measurable returns within months.

The first step is an asset inventory. List every piece of rotating or sliding equipment in your facility, identify all lubrication points, and record the manufacturer's recommended lubricant type, viscosity grade, and replenishment interval. Many facilities discover at this stage that they are using a dozen or more different lubricant grades where five or six would suffice — lubricant consolidation alone can reduce inventory costs and the risk of misapplication.

Next, establish a lubrication schedule with clear ownership. Assign specific tasks to named technicians, specify the lubricant product and quantity, and record each service event in your CMMS or maintenance log. Condition monitoring — checking oil color, viscosity, and particulate content — adds a further layer of protection by identifying degradation before it causes failure. Synthetic lubricants like Equipment Lubricant Extreme are particularly valuable in high-temperature or high-load applications, where they deliver significantly longer drain intervals and more consistent protection than mineral alternatives.

Finally, train your team. Correct lubrication technique — clean application tools, avoiding over-greasing bearings, using the right applicator for each point — is just as important as using the right product. A lubrication programme is only as good as the discipline with which it is executed.

title: Industrial Floor Coating Selection Guide: Epoxy, Polyurethane, and Beyond
summary: The floor coating market has expanded significantly in recent years. Understanding the differences between coating technologies helps facilities make better long-term investment decisions.
content:
Industrial floor coatings have evolved dramatically over the past decade. Where facilities once had limited choices between paint and bare concrete, today's market offers a wide spectrum of technologies — each with distinct performance profiles, application requirements, and cost structures. Making the right selection upfront avoids costly early failure and reapplication.

Epoxy coatings remain the workhorse of the industrial floor coating market. Two-component water-borne and solvent-borne epoxy systems deliver excellent chemical resistance, strong adhesion to prepared concrete, and good mechanical durability at a competitive cost. They are the standard choice for manufacturing floors, warehouses, automotive workshops, and food processing facilities. The primary limitation of epoxy is brittleness under thermal cycling and UV exposure — epoxy will chalk and yellow in outdoor or high-UV environments over time.

Polyurethane and polyaspartic topcoats are increasingly used as finish coats over epoxy primers. They offer superior UV stability, flexibility, and scratch resistance, making them ideal for areas with thermal cycling, direct sunlight, or aesthetics-critical environments such as showrooms and offices. The trade-off is higher material cost and a narrower application window for polyaspartic systems, which cure very rapidly.

For facilities handling aggressive chemicals — battery acid, strong solvents, or concentrated cleaning agents — vinyl ester and novolac epoxy systems provide the highest level of chemical resistance and are the only defensible choice for secondary containment areas. Specification and application of these systems requires careful attention to surface preparation and the environment during application, making experienced applicators essential.

title: Corrosion Prevention: Best Practices for Protecting Industrial Assets
summary: Corrosion is responsible for trillions of dollars in global economic losses each year. These practical strategies help industrial facilities protect their assets and extend service life.
content:
Corrosion is an electrochemical process that affects virtually every metal asset in an industrial facility — from structural steelwork and pipework to precision tooling and machinery. Left unmanaged, it shortens asset life, increases maintenance costs, creates safety hazards, and can result in catastrophic failures. The good news is that most corrosion is preventable with a systematic approach.

The foundation of any corrosion prevention strategy is a regular inspection programme. Visual inspection alone can identify early-stage surface rust, blistering of protective coatings, galvanic corrosion at dissimilar metal joints, and crevice corrosion in gaps and fastener holes. Early detection allows cost-effective remediation — treating light surface rust with a penetrating inhibitor like Rust Inhibitor Shield is far cheaper than replacing a corroded structural component.

For assets in high-humidity, coastal, or chemically aggressive environments, passive protection alone is rarely sufficient. A defence-in-depth approach combines surface preparation, primer, protective topcoat, and periodic inhibitor application. Ensure that any bare metal exposed during fabrication, cutting, or welding is treated with a corrosion inhibitor as quickly as possible — even a few hours of exposure in a humid environment can initiate rust that undermines subsequent coating adhesion.

Finally, consider your cleaning and maintenance protocols. Chloride contamination from cleaning products, process chemicals, or atmospheric deposition is a primary driver of corrosion under coatings and at cut edges. Use neutral or mildly alkaline cleaners on coated surfaces, rinse thoroughly, and ensure that surfaces dry quickly after cleaning. A well-maintained coating system combined with regular inhibitor top-up is the most cost-effective long-term corrosion management strategy available.
